title: Unwell After Overseas Travel with IV Drug Use (BBV / Infective Endocarditis)
patient_instructions: You are Jake, 28, who has felt progressively unwell and 'low in energy - I can hardly get out of bed' for a couple of weeks since returning from an overseas trip. You are guarded at first. Key hidden history to reveal ONLY when the candidate asks appropriately about drug use overseas: while away you used heroin for the first time, injected it, and shared needles with friends at a party. You feel very guilty and ashamed and may say 'it was my first time, I feel awful about it' - a good candidate should respond non-judgementally and explore your mood, sleep and coping. Sexual history: if asked only 'are you currently sexually active?' say 'no'; if the candidate also asks 'have you ever been sexually active?' say 'yes', with a past partner and inconsistent condom use. No tattoos, piercings or transfusions. Additional symptoms depend on what the candidate asks - reveal whichever the examiner directs for the running version (fever, sore throat, rash; or abdominal pain, dark urine, pale stools, jaundice, itch; or chest pain, breathlessness, racing heart). Affect: subdued, ashamed, worried you have caught something serious; reassured by a calm, respectful doctor.
candidate_instructions: You are a GP at a rural NSW practice. Jake, 28, presents feeling unwell and fatigued since returning from overseas. In 8 minutes: take a focused history of the unwell returned traveller, ensuring a sensitive and thorough drug, blood-borne-virus and sexual history; explore the psychosocial impact; generate and prioritise your differential; and request the targeted examination that will point to the diagnosis (the examiner will provide findings). Briefly outline your provisional diagnosis and immediate management/testing.
examiner_instructions: This history-taking station reframes 'unwell' once injecting drug use with needle sharing is elicited, towards blood-borne viruses and their complications. Choose ONE version and give findings accordingly: V1 Hepatitis (RUQ pain, jaundice, tender liver edge palpable 4-5 cm below costal margin, urine bilirubin+); V2 HIV seroconversion (rash, sore throat, cervical lymphadenopathy, aphthous ulcers); V3 infective endocarditis (in IVDU usually RIGHT-sided/tricuspid - pleuritic chest pain, cough, dyspnoea from septic pulmonary emboli, tricuspid pansystolic murmur; Staph aureus the usual organism). Reward: eliciting needle sharing; a full BBV/sexual history (never accepting 'not currently' - ask 'have you ever'); a non-judgemental response to guilt/shame with mood/coping screen; screening for HIV, hepatitis and endocarditis complications; and correct version-specific management. Correct the implausible 'liver span 22 cm'. Prompt if stuck: 'What is the most serious complication of injecting drug use you must exclude?'

criteria: Open start, clarifies 'unwell' (low energy, timing, functional impact)
Takes a structured travel and exposure history and elicits injecting heroin use with NEEDLE SHARING
Screens other blood-borne exposures (tattoos, piercings, transfusions) and food/water
Takes a thorough sexual history - does not accept 'not currently', asks 'have you ever been sexually active?', partners and condom use
Opens the psychosocial door non-judgementally, allays guilt/shame and screens mood, sleep and coping
Reframes the differential to blood-borne viruses (HIV, Hep B, Hep C) after needle sharing
Specifically screens for infective endocarditis as the key IVDU complication (chest pain, dyspnoea, palpitations, injection-site infection)
Requests targeted, version-appropriate examination and interprets the findings correctly
For endocarditis, recognises right-sided (tricuspid) IE with septic pulmonary emboli and Staphylococcus aureus as typical in IVDU
Arranges appropriate testing: 4th-generation HIV Ag/Ab assay with window-period counselling and repeat at ~6 weeks; Hep A/B/C serology (+ Hep E), consent and confidentiality
For endocarditis: three sets of blood cultures from separate sites before antibiotics, echocardiography (TTE/TOE) and modified Duke criteria
Harm reduction and public health: needle and syringe program referral, Hepatitis B vaccination, opioid dependence treatment, contact tracing/partner notification
Safety-net and urgent referral if features of sepsis, heart failure or fulminant hepatitis
Non-judgemental, respectful communication that supports disclosure of stigmatised behaviour
Explains the diagnosis, testing and plan in plain language and checks understanding

red_flags: Infective endocarditis in an injecting drug user - fever, new murmur, septic pulmonary emboli (pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea); Staphylococcus aureus, usually right-sided/tricuspid
Features of heart failure (raised JVP, crackles, peripheral oedema) or sepsis requiring urgent referral
HIV seroconversion illness (fever, rash, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, mucosal ulcers) after needle sharing and unsafe sex
Acute viral hepatitis with signs of fulminant hepatic failure (drowsiness, confusion, bleeding)
Suicidal ideation or severe guilt/shame in a distressed patient
australian_guidelines: ASHM / eTG HIV testing: use a 4th-generation HIV Ag/Ab combination assay, counsel on the window period and repeat testing at ~6 weeks; obtain informed consent and maintain confidentiality

eTG Antibiotic / Therapeutic Guidelines: for suspected infective endocarditis take three sets of blood cultures from separate sites before antibiotics, perform echocardiography and apply the modified Duke criteria
NSW Health / harm reduction: refer to a needle and syringe program, offer Hepatitis B vaccination and Hep A/B/C serology, and discuss opioid dependence (opioid substitution) treatment
Public Health Act (NSW): HIV and viral hepatitis are notifiable; undertake contact tracing / partner notification
eTG viral hepatitis: request Hep A IgM, HBsAg/anti-HBc IgM, anti-HCV with HCV RNA and Hep E serology in the at-risk traveller
learning_objectives: Take a sensitive, non-judgemental drug and sexual history that enables disclosure of stigmatised risk behaviour
Reframe the differential of the unwell patient after identifying injecting drug use with needle sharing
Recognise and investigate blood-borne viruses and infective endocarditis as complications of IVDU
Apply Australian HIV testing, harm-reduction and notification frameworks
Address the psychosocial impact (guilt, shame, mood) as part of holistic care
key_points: Never accept 'not currently' for a sexual or drug history - ask 'have you ever' to uncover past risk
In injecting drug users, infective endocarditis is typically right-sided (tricuspid) with septic pulmonary emboli, and Staphylococcus aureus is the usual organism
A stated 'liver span of 22 cm' is implausible - normal mid-clavicular span is ~6-12 cm; describe a tender liver edge palpable a few cm below the costal margin
Take three sets of blood cultures from separate sites BEFORE antibiotics when endocarditis is suspected
A non-judgemental response to guilt and shame is essential and directly enables accurate history taking

citations.claim: Injected heroin with shared needles is a major blood-borne-virus and infective-endocarditis risk that reframes the 'unwell' differential.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.317

citations.claim: Characterising stool as pale, fatty and offensive is an important clinical marker to elicit and distinguish - here supporting the cholestatic/hepatitis history in the hepatitis version.
Communication guidance to 'allay guilt', show interest and concern and be non-judgemental supports handling the patient's expressed guilt and shame.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.2014
